idiom_name: plain {rel, href, method} link objects + new URL(ref, base) + fetch(link.href)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no link-with-metadata type, so the idiom is a plain object literal - { rel, href, type?, method? } - embedded HAL-style under _links, with the WHATWG URL global (browsers, workers, and Node's node:url) standing in for a URI class: new URL(ref, base) resolves relative references against the request origin, percent-encodes path segments, and throws TypeError on malformed input (URL.canParse for non-throwing guards). The consumer dereferences with fetch(link.href), which returns a Promise<Response>; fetch rejects only on network failure or an invalid URL, so link rot surfaces as response.ok === false, not as an exception. These two primitives replace the classic producer/carrier/consumer/resolver component structure with ordinary functions over literals. The full classic form is still justified when links must ride the RFC 8288 Link header - response.headers.get('Link') is only a raw string, so header parsing and rel-graph traversal (Ketting, @windyroad/fetch-link) are library territory, not hand-rolled code.
pitfalls: fetch() does not reject on HTTP error statuses: a dangling link resolves to a 404/410 Response with ok === false, and code that calls res.json() without checking throws an opaque SyntaxError far from the link that caused it.

String-built hrefs ('/api/orders/' + id + '/pay') skip percent-encoding and drift from the API base across environments; construct with new URL(ref, base) and guard with URL.canParse so a malformed reference fails at creation, not at dereference time.

Issuing absolute links from internal service hostnames and ports exposes topology to untrusted clients; derive the external base from the inbound request origin (new URL(request.url).origin) or emit relative references resolved against a documented base.

An href is not an authorization grant: fetch defaults to credentials: 'same-origin', so ambient cookies ride along on followed links, and a link forwarded from a trusted context confers no rights - enforce authorization at resolution time on the server.

Acting on a link without checking rel and method: a link tagged 'related' is not licensed for mutation - validate the relation (prefer IANA-registered rels) against the intended operation before dereferencing.
response.headers.get('Link') is a single raw string; hand-rolled parsers routinely mishandle quoted parameters and commas inside URIs - use a maintained RFC 8288 parser instead of a split(',').

Following links recursively without a visited Set: object identity does not survive JSON round-trips, so cycle detection must compare hrefs - otherwise a link loop fans out into unbounded fetch chains.
